title: Act II, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: A drunken Porter imagines himself porter of hell gate, joking about a farmer, an 'equivocator' and a tailor, before opening to Macduff and Lennox. Lennox describes an unruly night of storms and screams. Macduff discovers Duncan's body ('Confusion now hath made his masterpiece!'). Macbeth reveals he has killed the chamberlains, claiming fury and love; Lady Macbeth faints. Banquo vows to fight 'treasonous malice.' Malcolm and Donalbain secretly flee to England and Ireland, fearing 'daggers in men's smiles.'

context.history: The Porter's 'equivocator' is widely read as an allusion to the Jesuit Henry Garnet, executed in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot, who defended misleading answers under oath.

significance: Comic relief deepens the horror: the castle has become hell's gate. Macbeth's killing of the grooms removes witnesses and makes his own guilt more visible; the princes' flight lets suspicion fall on them.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

contentNotes.teacherNote: The Porter jokes about 'a farmer, that hanged himself on the expectation of plenty' and about drink, which 'provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance' (lechery). Gloss the innuendo briefly; do not have students perform it. Then Duncan's body is discovered and Macbeth kills the grooms. Use the safe-messaging script for the suicide joke.

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.

framing.script: Teacher reads aloud before the reading. What happens: This scene has a joke about suicide, crude drinking jokes, and the discovery of a murder. Support is available if this is hard to read. Context: Recurring violence (murders on and off stage, including a child), witchcraft, a reported suicide and a severed head; the play's treatment of 'manhood' and of Lady Macbeth draws on period gender ideas that deserve critical discussion. See the scene notes and the safe-messaging script. Self-harm is wrong, and it is never the answer to pain; the story shows its cost, not a solution.
